common_name: Longfellow Chewings Fescue (Original Fine-Textured Shade Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall into a well-prepared seedbed; Longfellow was one of the earlier named Chewings fescue cultivars bred for fine texture and shade performance before being succeeded by the improved Longfellow II.

directions: Longfellow is a bunch-type Chewings fescue cultivar valued for its narrow, fine-bladed leaves and strong tolerance of the dry shade under mature trees where Kentucky bluegrass and tall fescue typically thin out. It tolerates low fertility, infrequent mowing, and acidic soils better than most cool-season turf species, making it a mainstay of low-input shade lawn mixes. Its main drawback is the same limitation shared by all fine fescues: it spreads only slowly by tillering rather than by rhizomes, so it cannot repair bare or worn patches on its own and thin areas need to be overseeded. By the time newer disease-resistant fine fescue cultivars such as Longfellow II reached the market, Longfellow had already established a long track record in regional variety trials as a dependable, if increasingly dated, standard for shaded cool-season lawns.

common_name: Accolade Cherry (Early-Blooming Semi-Double Pink Flowering Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Accolade is a hybrid raised in England from Sargent cherry crossed with Prunus subhirtella and blooms earlier than most ornamental cherries.

directions: Accolade was raised by British plantsman Collingwood Ingram from a cross between Sargent cherry (Prunus sargentii) and the autumn-flowering Higan cherry (Prunus subhirtella), combining the cold hardiness and vigor of its Sargent parent with the graceful, semi-pendulous branching of Higan cherry. In early spring, well before most other ornamental cherries open, it covers its bare branches in drooping clusters of large, semi-double, soft pink flowers that fade gently as they age, giving an unusually long and showy bloom display for a flowering cherry. The tree develops a broad, rounded, spreading crown on a single trunk with attractive reddish-brown bark, and its foliage turns respectable shades of orange and bronze in fall. It is faster-growing and generally more floriferous at a young age than many other flowering cherry cultivars, making it a popular choice for specimen planting in lawns and along streets in climates too cold for the more tender Yoshino and Kwanzan cherries.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water.

directions: Aechmea fosteriana is a Brazilian bromeliad species named for pioneering bromeliad breeder Mulford Foster, prized for its thick, stiff, olive-green to coppery-bronze leaves mottled and speckled with irregular darker brown blotches, an understated but distinctive pattern that intensifies under brighter indirect light. Its low, tank-forming rosette holds water at the base the way most Aechmeas do, so it should be kept filled and periodically flushed to prevent stagnation. A stout, upright spike of small flowers set among pink to coral bracts emerges from the center of a mature rosette. Beyond its own quiet ornamental value, this species is historically significant as breeding stock: crossed with the more boldly patterned Aechmea orlandiana, it produced Foster's classic 1945 hybrid 'Bert', and its genes persist in numerous other named Foster-line Aechmea hybrids grown today.
